items.text: Nipple: Contains the openings of the lactiferous ducts.
Areola: Pigmented skin surrounding the nipple.
Glandular tissue: Lobules produce milk; ducts transport it towards the nipple.
Cooper's ligaments: Fibrous supporting structures that help maintain breast shape.
Retromammary space: Allows the breast some mobility over the pectoral fascia.
Axillary tail of Spence: Extension of breast tissue towards the axilla.

blocks.text: Divide each breast into four quadrants using vertical and horizontal lines through the nipple:

items.text: Upper outer quadrant.
Upper inner quadrant.
Lower outer quadrant.
Lower inner quadrant.

blocks.text: Also examine the central or retroareolar region and the axillary tail.
The upper outer quadrant contains a substantial amount of breast tissue and is a common site for breast cancers. However, malignancy can arise in any region.

items.text: Axillary lymph nodes receive most lymphatic drainage from the breast.
Internal mammary or parasternal nodes receive drainage from medial breast regions.
Supraclavicular and infraclavicular nodes may be relevant in advanced or regional disease.

blocks.text: This is why a breast examination must include appropriate regional lymph node assessment.
Breast examination requires particular attention to privacy, dignity and informed consent.

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the purpose and steps of the examination.
Obtain informed consent.
Offer a chaperone and follow local policy.
Ask about pain before touching the breasts.
Provide adequate privacy and expose only the area necessary.
Examine both breasts, even if the complaint affects only one side.

blocks.text: Position the patient initially sitting upright, with the upper body appropriately exposed. You will later ask the patient to lie supine for palpation.

items.text: Breast lump: onset, duration, growth and associated pain.
Breast pain: location, timing and relationship to menstruation.
Nipple discharge: spontaneous or expressed, unilateral or bilateral, colour and whether bloody.
Nipple inversion or recent changes.
Skin changes, ulceration or dimpling.
Fever, redness or symptoms suggesting infection.
Pregnancy, lactation and menstrual history where relevant.
Previous breast disease, surgery, biopsy or implants.
Family history of breast or ovarian cancer and relevant genetic risk.
Current medications, including hormonal treatment.

blocks.text: Red flags: A new suspicious breast lump, spontaneous unilateral bloody discharge, new nipple inversion, skin tethering, peau d'orange or suspicious axillary nodes warrants prompt assessment.
Inspection is performed with the patient sitting upright. Examine both breasts together and compare their size, shape, contour, skin and nipples.

content_groups.group_title: A. Inspect with the arms relaxed

blocks.text: Ask the patient to sit with the arms relaxed by the sides.
Inspect the following:
1. Breast size and symmetry

items.text: Normal: Breasts may differ slightly in size, but there is no new or suspicious asymmetry.
Abnormal: New unilateral enlargement, distortion or a change in breast contour.

blocks.text: Mild asymmetry is common and does not automatically indicate disease.
2. Breast contour

items.text: Normal: Smooth contour without focal distortion.
Abnormal: Localized bulging, flattening, distortion or visible retraction.

blocks.text: 3. Skin

items.text: Normal: Skin is intact, without focal dimpling, ulceration or abnormal erythema.
Abnormal: Dimpling, tethering, redness, thickening, ulceration or oedema.

blocks.text: Skin dimpling may result from traction on Cooper's ligaments by an underlying lesion.
4. Visible veins

items.text: Normal: No new prominent or asymmetric superficial venous pattern.
Abnormal: Prominent unilateral superficial veins may accompany increased vascularity or an underlying mass. Interpret this alongside the rest of the examination.

blocks.text: 5. Nipple position and direction

items.text: Normal: Nipples may naturally differ slightly in position, but there is no new distortion.
Abnormal: New inversion, retraction, deviation or asymmetry.

blocks.text: A long-standing, stable inverted nipple may be normal for that patient. New inversion is more concerning.
6. Areola

items.text: Normal: No suspicious ulceration, crusting, scaling or distortion.
Abnormal: Persistent eczematous changes, ulceration or an altered areolar appearance.

blocks.text: Persistent unilateral nipple or areolar eczema requires assessment for conditions such as Paget disease of the breast.

content_groups.group_title: B. Inspect with the arms raised

blocks.text: Ask the patient to raise both arms above the head.
Observe whether the breasts move symmetrically and whether any area of skin or nipple is pulled inwards.

items.text: Normal: No focal distortion or skin tethering becomes apparent.
Abnormal: A localized area may become visibly retracted as the breasts are elevated.

blocks.text: This manoeuvre can reveal subtle tethering that was not obvious at rest.

content_groups.group_title: C. Ask the patient to press their hands against their hips

blocks.text: Ask the patient to place both hands on their hips and press firmly, contracting the pectoral muscles.
Alternatively, ask them to press their palms together in front of the chest.

items.text: Skin dimpling.
Fixation of a mass to deeper structures.
Asymmetry or distortion of the breast contour.

blocks.text: Interpretation: A lesion that becomes more visibly tethered during pectoral contraction may be attached to deeper tissues. This is concerning but is not diagnostic of malignancy by itself.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Inspection of the nipple and areola

blocks.text: Inspect both nipples carefully before palpation.

items.text: Position and symmetry.
Inversion or retraction.
Crusting, scaling or ulceration.
Discharge visible at the nipple.
Changes in the areola.
Any obvious mass beneath the nipple.
Inversion: The nipple turns inward.
Retraction: The nipple is pulled inward or deviated, often because of traction on underlying tissues.

blocks.text: These terms are sometimes used interchangeably clinically, but the important distinction is whether the change is new and associated with other suspicious features.
Do not routinely squeeze a normal nipple to elicit discharge.
If discharge is reported or observed, characterize it by asking whether it is:

items.text: Spontaneous or only expressed.
Unilateral or bilateral.
From one duct or multiple ducts.
Bloody, serous, milky, purulent or another colour.

blocks.text: Spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct bloody or serous discharge is more concerning for underlying ductal pathology and warrants assessment.
Milky discharge may be associated with pregnancy, lactation, medication effects or hyperprolactinaemia. Purulent discharge with pain and erythema may suggest infection.
OSCE point: Document the character and laterality of discharge rather than simply recording “nipple discharge present.”
Palpation is performed systematically to ensure that no area of breast tissue is missed.
Ask the patient to lie supine.

items.text: For examining the right breast, place the right arm above the head.
For examining the left breast, place the left arm above the head.
A small pillow or folded towel beneath the shoulder on the side being examined can help spread the breast tissue across the chest wall.

blocks.text: Ensure the patient is comfortable and explain each step before proceeding.
Use the palmar pads of the middle three fingers, keeping them relatively flat against the breast.
Apply light, medium and deeper pressure to assess superficial, intermediate and deeper tissues.
Avoid pinching the breast between your fingers, because this can make normal tissue feel falsely nodular.

content_groups.group_title: Step 3: Choose a systematic palpation pattern

blocks.text: Any consistent pattern that covers the entire breast is acceptable.
Vertical strip pattern
Move up and down in parallel strips, from the clavicle to the inframammary fold and from the sternum to the midaxillary line. This is a useful systematic approach.
Circular pattern
Palpate in progressively larger or smaller circles, ensuring complete coverage.
Radial or wedge pattern
Examine from the nipple outwards along each wedge, covering the entire breast.

items.text: The clavicle superiorly.
The inframammary fold inferiorly.
The sternum medially.
The midaxillary line laterally.

blocks.text: Do not forget the axillary tail of Spence, which extends towards the axilla.
Palpate the central breast and retroareolar region gently. Examine both breasts even if the patient reports a unilateral lump.
If a lump is detected, characterize it using the following framework.
1. Site
Specify the breast, quadrant and distance from the nipple.
Example: Right upper outer quadrant, 3 cm from the nipple.
2. Size and shape
Measure the approximate dimensions in centimetres, preferably in two perpendicular planes. Describe the shape as round, oval or irregular.
3. Surface and consistency
Describe the surface as smooth or irregular and the consistency as soft, firm, hard or cystic.
4. Tenderness and mobility
Establish whether the lump is tender and whether it moves freely over the surrounding breast tissue and deeper chest wall.
5. Relationship to surrounding structures
Assess for skin tethering, nipple distortion, attachment to the chest wall and associated regional lymphadenopathy.
Try to move the mass gently in different directions.

items.text: Freely mobile: The mass moves relative to surrounding structures.
Restricted mobility: The mass moves less freely than expected.
Fixed: The mass appears attached to skin or deeper tissues.

blocks.text: A mass fixed to the chest wall may be associated with advanced malignancy or other causes of adhesion. Clinical mobility alone cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant disease.

content_groups.group_title: Step 7: Assess for tenderness and temperature

blocks.text: Ask whether the patient feels pain as you palpate.

items.text: Normal: No focal tenderness.
Abnormal: Tenderness may occur with mastitis, an abscess, trauma or other conditions.

blocks.text: Compare the temperature of the breasts if infection is suspected. Warmth, erythema and tenderness together support an inflammatory process but do not establish the cause.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. Special examination of a suspected breast lump

blocks.text: When a lump is present, several additional manoeuvres help assess its relationship to surrounding structures.
Observe whether the skin is pulled inward over the lump. Gentle movement of the skin over the mass may help assess whether the lesion is attached to it.
Skin tethering can occur when a lesion involves or shortens the supporting fibrous structures.
Ask the patient to press their hands against their hips or contract the pectoral muscles.
Observe and palpate whether the mass becomes less mobile or more firmly attached to the chest wall during contraction.
This may suggest deeper fixation but is not diagnostic on its own.
If the lump feels cystic, assess gently for fluctuation.

items.text: A fluctuant lump may contain fluid.
A tense cyst or abscess may not be obviously fluctuant.

blocks.text: Ultrasound is more reliable than palpation alone for determining whether a lesion is cystic or solid.
Assess gently if clinically appropriate.
Compressibility may occur with some vascular lesions or other soft masses, but it is not a routine diagnostic test for every breast lump.

A cough impulse is not a routine or useful discriminator for ordinary breast lumps. Do not perform it unless there is a specific clinical reason to suspect a lesion with a connection to another anatomical space.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. Examination of the axillary lymph nodes

blocks.text: This is an essential component of breast examination because the axilla is a major route of breast lymphatic drainage.

items.text: Keep the patient sitting upright.
Explain what you are going to do and ensure appropriate exposure.
Support the patient's arm so that the shoulder muscles are relaxed.
Insert the finger pads high into the axilla.
Palpate the axillary contents systematically, bringing the fingers down along the chest wall where appropriate.
Repeat on the other side.

rows: At the apex of the axilla

blocks.text: For every enlarged node, document its location, number, size, consistency, tenderness, mobility and matting.
“No significant palpable axillary lymphadenopathy bilaterally.”

items.text: Tender, mobile nodes may occur with infection or inflammation.
Hard, fixed or irregular nodes raise concern for malignancy.
Enlarged nodes in a patient with a suspicious breast mass require further assessment.

blocks.text: Examine the supraclavicular and infraclavicular regions as well. Consider the internal mammary nodes when clinically relevant; these are not usually accessible to routine palpation.

subsections.subsection_title: 8. Examination of the supraclavicular and infraclavicular nodes

blocks.text: medistudents.com

items.text: Palpate both supraclavicular fossae immediately above the clavicles.
Examine the infraclavicular regions below the clavicles where appropriate.
Compare both sides.
Normal: No palpable pathological lymphadenopathy.
Abnormal: Enlarged, hard or fixed nodes may indicate significant underlying pathology, including malignancy.

blocks.text: Exam point: A breast examination should not end after palpating the axilla. Always assess the supraclavicular regions, particularly if malignancy is suspected.
Male breast examination follows the same core principles: inspection, palpation, nipple assessment and regional lymph node examination.

items.text: Asymmetry or enlargement.
Nipple inversion or discharge.
Skin changes, ulceration or tethering.
A discrete mass.

blocks.text: Palpate the breast tissue and retroareolar region.
Gynaecomastia commonly presents as a concentric, rubbery or firm disc of tissue beneath the nipple and areola. It may be unilateral or bilateral and may be tender.
Male breast cancer may present as a hard, irregular, eccentric mass, sometimes with nipple retraction, discharge, skin changes or axillary lymphadenopathy.
These patterns overlap, so a suspicious male breast mass requires appropriate investigation.
If gynaecomastia is suspected, examine for testicular masses and features of relevant endocrine, hepatic or systemic disease. Review medications and other potential causes.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Clinical patterns: benign versus concerning findings

blocks.text: Fibroadenoma
Often a well-circumscribed, firm or rubbery, mobile and painless lump, particularly in younger women.
A typical examination cannot definitively establish fibroadenoma; imaging and sometimes biopsy are needed.
Breast cyst
May feel smooth, well-defined and fluctuant, and can be tender.
Ultrasound helps distinguish a simple cyst from a solid or complex lesion.
Mastitis
Pain, warmth, erythema and tenderness, sometimes accompanied by fever, particularly during lactation.
A persistent or progressive mass requires assessment for abscess or another diagnosis.
Breast abscess
Localized painful swelling, often with erythema and warmth; fluctuation may be present.
Ultrasound can identify a collection that may require drainage.
Possible breast malignancy
May present as a hard, irregular, poorly mobile lump, skin tethering, new nipple retraction or suspicious lymphadenopathy.
Breast cancer may also present with a painless, mobile or otherwise subtle mass; absence of classic signs does not exclude it.

items.text: Skin dimpling or tethering.
New nipple inversion or deviation.
Peau d'orange — skin resembling orange peel due to oedema around hair follicles.
A hard or irregular mass.
Suspicious axillary or supraclavicular nodes.
Persistent unilateral nipple or areolar eczema.
Spontaneous unilateral bloody discharge.
Ulceration or progressive distortion of the breast.

blocks.text: No single finding confirms malignancy. A suspicious clinical examination must be followed by appropriate investigations.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. The triple assessment of a breast lump

blocks.text: One of the most important breast examination topics for clinical and postgraduate examinations is triple assessment.
1. Clinical assessment
Focused history and physical examination of both breasts and regional lymph nodes.
2. Imaging
Diagnostic breast imaging, using ultrasound, mammography or both as appropriate to age, pregnancy status, symptoms and local protocols.
3. Tissue diagnosis
Image-guided core needle biopsy is commonly used when a suspicious solid lesion requires histological diagnosis.
The results should be assessed together. If the examination is suspicious but imaging is reassuring, further evaluation may still be necessary.

blocks.title: Depending on the clinical picture, the specialist may request:

items.text: Ultrasound of the axilla or other regional nodes.
Biopsy of suspicious lymph nodes.
Additional imaging for staging after a cancer diagnosis.
Hormonal or other laboratory investigations for selected conditions.

blocks.text: Tumour markers are not appropriate as a stand-alone test to diagnose a new breast lump.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. How to present normal breast findings

blocks.text: Normal OSCE presentation

“On inspection, both breasts are symmetrical, with no visible masses, skin dimpling, erythema or nipple abnormalities. On palpation, there are no discrete masses or areas of focal tenderness in either breast. There is no significant palpable axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.”
Copy normal presentation

Only include findings that you actually assessed. If the patient reports discharge, do not document “no nipple abnormalities” without clarifying the discharge history and relevant examination findings.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. How to present abnormal breast findings

blocks.text: A. Suspected fibroadenoma

“There is a discrete lump in the left upper outer quadrant, approximately 2 cm from the nipple, measuring about 2 cm in diameter. It is smooth, well-circumscribed, firm, non-tender and freely mobile. There are no associated skin changes, nipple abnormalities or palpable regional lymph nodes.”
Interpretation: The clinical features may be consistent with a benign breast lesion such as fibroadenoma, but further assessment is required.
Copy presentation
B. Suspicious breast lump

“There is a hard, irregular mass in the right upper outer quadrant, measuring approximately [size] cm. It is poorly mobile and associated with [skin tethering/nipple retraction, if present]. There are [number and description] palpable right axillary lymph nodes. These findings are suspicious for malignancy and warrant urgent triple assessment.”
Copy presentation
C. Acute mastitis

“The [right/left] breast is erythematous, warm and tender, with localized swelling involving the [location]. There is [no palpable collection/a suspected localized collection]. I would assess the patient's temperature, systemic condition and lactation history, and consider ultrasound if an abscess is suspected.”
Copy presentation
D. Nipple discharge

“There is [spontaneous/expressed] discharge from the [right/left/both] nipple. The discharge is [colour], arising from [one/multiple] ducts. Associated findings include [mass, nipple changes, skin changes or lymphadenopathy]. I would investigate further according to the discharge characteristics and clinical findings.”
Copy presentation
Use this checklist to practise the entire examination from beginning to end.
Introduce yourself, explain the examination and obtain consent
Offer a chaperone and ensure privacy
Ask about pain and relevant breast symptoms
Inspect both breasts with arms relaxed
Inspect with arms raised
Ask the patient to press hands against hips or contract pectoral muscles
Inspect nipples and areolae
Position the patient supine and support the shoulder if needed
Palpate all quadrants of both breasts systematically
Examine the central breast and retroareolar region
Examine the axillary tail of Spence
Characterize any lump by site, size, shape, surface, consistency, tenderness and mobility
Assess skin tethering and attachment to deeper structures if indicated
Examine both axillae
Examine supraclavicular and infraclavicular regions
Thank the patient, cover them and wash your hands
Present findings and recommend appropriate further assessment
1. Why must both breasts be examined?
To compare sides, identify asymmetry, detect additional lesions and avoid missing a contralateral abnormality.
2. What is peau d'orange?
An orange-peel appearance of the skin caused by dermal oedema, often due to impaired lymphatic drainage. In the breast, it can be a sign of malignancy.
3. What is the significance of skin dimpling?
It may indicate traction on Cooper's ligaments by an underlying lesion, including breast cancer.
4. What is the difference between fibroadenoma and breast carcinoma on examination?

Fibroadenomas are often smooth, well-circumscribed, firm and mobile. Carcinomas may be hard, irregular and poorly mobile, with skin or nipple changes. There is substantial overlap, so clinical examination cannot definitively distinguish them.
5. What is triple assessment?
Clinical assessment, breast imaging and tissue diagnosis when indicated.
6. Why examine the axilla?
To identify regional lymphadenopathy, which may reflect infection, inflammation or metastatic spread from breast malignancy.
7. What is Paget disease of the breast?

A condition involving malignant cells in the nipple epidermis, often associated with underlying ductal carcinoma. It may present with persistent unilateral nipple eczema, scaling, crusting or ulceration.
8. What is the significance of a new inverted nipple?
It may indicate underlying breast pathology, including malignancy, and requires assessment, particularly if unilateral or associated with a mass.
9. Can a painful breast lump be malignant?
Yes. Pain does not exclude malignancy.
10. What would you do if clinical examination is suspicious but the ultrasound is normal?
Reassess the clinical and imaging findings together and arrange further specialist evaluation. A suspicious examination should not be dismissed solely because initial imaging is reassuring.
For breast examination, remember this sequence:
Inspect → Palpate both breasts → Characterize any lump → Examine axillary and supraclavicular nodes → Present findings → Recommend triple assessment when indicated.
Always prioritize patient consent, dignity and comfort, and never reassure a patient about a suspicious mass based on palpation alone.
